Quant à « seul le temps nous fait périr », Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid et Qatada l'expliquent par le cours des jours, des nuits et la longueur de la vie, Qatada ajoutant le sens d'âge, Qutrub y voyant la mort, et 'Ikrima celui de Dieu. Tous s'accordent à y voir un déni de l'au-delà et une opinion fondée sur la conjecture et non sur la science. Plusieurs, dont al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et al-Nasafi, rapportent le hadith « Ne maudissez pas le temps, car Dieu est le Temps » et expliquent que la cause véritable est Dieu, à qui la faute revient. Ibn al-Jawzi précise que Dieu est celui qui fait périr, non le temps qu'on imagine. Les commentateurs s'accordent enfin à dire que Dieu leur oppose l'absence de tout savoir fondé et que leur seul argument, réclamer le retour de leurs ancêtres, appelle la réponse : Dieu fait vivre et mourir, puis rassemble les hommes pour le Jour de la Résurrection, qui ne fait aucun doute.

Ce passage décrit l'attitude des polythéistes qui nient la résurrection : lorsque leur sont récitées des versets clairs sur la résurrection, leur seul argument est de dire au Prophète : fais revenir nos ancêtres morts, si tu dis vrai. Al-Zamakhshari et Ibn 'Atiyya expliquent que l'on appelle cela « argument » par dérision, puisque ce n'en est pas un, et qu'il faut comprendre qu'ils n'en ont aucun. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Juzayy et Ibn Sa'di rattachent leur croyance au doute et à la conjecture, et relèvent que la négation de la résurrection s'accompagne chez certains d'une négation du Créateur, attribuant la vie et la mort au temps (ad-dahr). Al-Tabari et al-Baghawi comprennent la réponse divine comme affirmant que Dieu fait vivre et mourir, puis rassemble les hommes au Jour de la résurrection ; celui qui crée une première fois peut recréer. Al-Razi et al-Qurtubi ajoutent que l'homme passe par des étapes, de la poussière à la goutte de sperme, ce qui témoigne de la capacité divine à recréer.

Les commentateurs divergent sur plusieurs points. Certains, comme al-Mawardi et Ibn Juzayy, expliquent « nous mourons et nous vivons » de façons diverses : meurent certains et vivent d'autres, meurent les pères et vivent les enfants, ou il y a inversion dans l'ordre des mots. Al-Razi relève aussi que l'argument des adversaires est faible, car ce qui n'a pas lieu maintenant n'est pas pour autant impossible, puisque nous n'existions pas avant notre naissance. Abu Hayyan et al-Alusi discutent de la grammaire de « hujjatahum » et notent que les interprétations sont multiples. Ibn 'Ashur conclut que ce discours est une manière de se dérober à la preuve claire.

Ce passage répond aux négateurs de la résurrection parmi les Qurayshites, qui affirmaient que la vie se réduit à la vie d'ici-bas, que nous mourons et vivons sans autre destin, que c'est le temps qui nous fait périr, et qu'ils réclamaient le retour de leurs ancêtres comme preuve. Les commentateurs expliquent que le verset « Dis : c'est Allah qui vous donne la vie, puis vous fait mourir, puis vous rassemblera le jour de la Résurrection, qui ne fait aucun doute » signifie que c'est Allah, et non le temps, qui fait vivre et mourir. Al-Tabari et Ibn Kathir y voient l'affirmation que celui qui a créé au commencement peut recréer, et que le rassemblement a lieu pour la rétribution. Az-Zamakhshari et Abu Hayyan présentent le verset comme une réfutation par leurs propres aveux : ils reconnaissent qu'Allah les fait vivre et mourir, et celui qui en est capable peut aussi ramener leurs ancêtres. Les avis divergent sur le sens du mot « ad-dahr » : Mujahid y voit le temps, Qatada la durée de la vie, Abu Qutrub la mort, et Ikrima Allah lui-même. Ibn Kathir rapporte le hadith « Ne maudissez pas le temps, car Allah est le temps », qu'il interprète comme signifiant que l'action attribuée au temps revient en réalité à Allah. Plusieurs commentateurs, dont al-Razi et al-Baghawi, soulignent que la majorité des gens ne savent pas, faute de réflexion sur les signes, et que leur doute ne vient pas d'une véritable incertitude sur la résurrection.

Ce verset affirme que la royauté sur les cieux et la terre appartient à Dieu seul, qui en dispose à sa guise, et annonce que le jour où l'Heure se dressera, les tenants de l'erreur seront les perdants. Al-Tabari explique que ces derniers sont les associateurs et ceux qui adorent d'autres divinités, et que leur perte consiste à voir les croyants recevoir les demeures du Paradis tandis qu'ils héritent de places en Enfer. Ibn Kathir précise qu'il s'agit des mécréants qui rejettent les signes et les preuves envoyés par Dieu, et Ibn 'Atiyya relie le passage à la contestation des Quraych qui demandaient qu'on ressuscite leurs ancêtres. Les commentateurs s'accordent sur le sens général de la perte et de la révélation de l'erreur au jour du jugement. Ils divergent sur la construction grammaticale: Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan et al-Qurtubi expliquent que le verbe « yakhsaru » gouverne la proposition temporelle et que « yawma'idhin » est une apposition ou une insistance, tandis que d'autres font dépendre le temps de l'idée de royauté. Les versets suivants, que plusieurs commentateurs rattachent à celui-ci, décrivent les nations agenouillées, appelées à leur livre d'actes, dont les diverses interprétations opposent certains à d'autres. Al-Mawardi recense plusieurs sens du mot « jathiya » (agenouillée, rassemblée, soumise), tandis qu'al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et al-Baghawi retiennent surtout la position à genoux. Sur le « livre » auquel on est appelé, Ibn Kathir et al-Baghawi y voient le registre des actes, alors qu'Ibn 'Ashur y voit plutôt la loi révélée à chaque communauté.

Ce verset décrit la scène du Jour de la Résurrection : on voit chaque communauté rassemblée, agenouillée (jathiya), dans l'attente du jugement, signe de l'effroi et de la soumission. Mujahid, Qatada, al-Hasan, al-Dahhak et Ibn Zayd comprennent cette posture comme le fait d'être à genoux, certains précisant qu'il s'agit de la position de celui qui est prêt à se relever (istifaz). Ibn Abbas l'interprète comme « réunis », 'Ikrima comme « distincts », Mu'arrij comme « humbles » selon le dialecte des Quraysh. Al-Zamakhshari et Ibn 'Atiyya relèvent que le verbe jadhw est encore plus expressif que jathw. Al-Qurtubi et al-Baghawi rapportent le propos de Salman al-Farisi selon lequel, durant une heure des plus terribles de ce jour, les gens se mettent à genoux, jusqu'à Abraham.

Quant à « chaque communauté est appelée à son livre », les avis se répartissent. Ibn Abbas et Abu Salih y voient le registre des actes, bons et mauvais, tandis que Qatada et Mujahid rattachent ce livre à ce que les anges y consignaient. Al-Sha'bi, al-Farra' et Ibn Qutayba y voient le compte à rendre. Yahya ibn Sallam estime qu'il s'agit du Livre révélé à chaque communauté, afin de vérifier si elle l'a suivi, et Ibn Jarir inclut aussi les Écritures révélées. Ibn Juzayy et Ibn Sa'di tiennent les deux sens possibles, Ibn 'Ashur rappelant que le pluriel indéfini favorise le sens des Livres révélés. Al-Razi, al-Nasafi et Abu al-Su'ud retiennent surtout le registre des actes.

Sur le « istinsakh », la plupart des commentateurs, dont Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi et al-Qurtubi, comprennent que Dieu ordonne aux anges de consigner les actes, certains précisant qu'ils recopient ce qui est dans la Table préservée. Ibn 'Abbas, cité par Ibn Kathir et al-Alusi, défend ce sens en affirmant que la copie suppose un original. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan et Ibn 'Ashur examinent le sens exact du mot nasakh, certains y voyant la simple écriture et d'autres la reproduction à partir d'un modèle.

Ce verset fait partie de la description du Jour du Jugement : chaque communauté est vue à genoux et appelée à son livre, et ce livre déclare, en toute vérité, qu'il consigne ce que les gens ont fait. La plupart des commentateurs s'accordent à y voir le registre des actes, et comprennent que le livre « parle contre vous » parce qu'il montre exactement ce qui a été accompli, sans rien ajouter ni omettre. Ibn Kathir et al-Baghawi identifient ce livre au registre tenu par les anges gardiens, et al-Tabari rapporte d'après Ibn Abbas qu'il contient les actes des fils d'Adam. D'autres savants désignent un autre livre : Mujahid et Muqatil, selon al-Mawardi et Ibn al-Jawzi, y voient la Tablette préservée, qui atteste de la destinée de chacun, tandis qu'Ibn Qutayba y voit le Coran, qui rappelle les actes. Ibn Juzayy retient la première interprétation. Le terme « nastansikh » est expliqué de plusieurs façons. Ibn Abbas, al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi et Ibn Kathir rapportent que les anges copient à partir d'un original, la Tablette préservée ou la Mère du Livre, puis confrontent les registres des gardiens à cette copie, Ibn Abbas arguant que la copie suppose toujours un modèle. Al-Baghawi et al-Qurtubi mentionnent aussi que les feuillets des actes sont remontés et que seuls ceux qui méritent récompense ou châtiment sont retenus. Al-Dahhak y voit le sens de « faire subsister », al-Suddi celui d'écrire, et al-Hasan celui de conserver. Ibn al-Qayyim estime que les deux sens peuvent être visés, tandis qu'al-Nasafi entend simplement une mise par écrit, sans copie d'un modèle.

Ce verset décrit le sort des croyants qui ont accompli de bonnes œuvres le jour de la résurrection : Dieu les fait entrer dans Sa miséricorde. La plupart des commentateurs, comme Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya et al-Nasafi, entendent par cette miséricorde le Paradis, et Ibn Kathir s'appuie sur le hadith où Dieu dit au Paradis : « Tu es Ma miséricorde ». Al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari et Ibn al-Jawzi expliquent que les croyants sont ceux qui ont affirmé l'unicité de Dieu et obéi à Ses ordres et évité Ses interdits, et que leur entrée dans la miséricorde est l'obtention de ce qu'ils recherchaient dans cette vie. Abu al-Su'ud et al-Shawkani y voient une précision de ce qui arrive aux communautés après le rappel de leur promesse et de leur menace. Tous s'accordent à dire que le succès éclatant est une réussite manifeste à laquelle rien ne succède. Al-Biqa'i précise qu'elle est claire parce qu'elle n'est mêlée d'aucun trouble, contrairement aux réussites d'ici-bas, qui restaient obscures pour ceux qui n'avaient pas la certitude. Al-Razi établit une distinction entre la foi et les bonnes œuvres, qu'il considère comme un élément distinct qui s'ajoute à la foi, et il relève que les Mu'tazilites tirent de la formule une lecture différente de la sienne sur la condition d'accès au Paradis. Il note également que le mot « miséricorde » suppose que la récompense n'est pas due. Al-Sa'di et Ibn 'Ashur expliquent que l'expression « entrer dans Sa miséricorde » englobe toutes les formes de bienfaits que l'âme peut concevoir, la miséricorde étant présentée comme un lieu où l'on entre. Le passage s'inscrit dans le contexte du jugement dernier et de la rétribution.

Ce verset décrit le sort des mécréants le Jour de la Résurrection : il leur sera dit, sur le mode du reproche et de la réprimande, « Mes versets ne vous étaient-ils pas récités ? Mais vous vous êtes enflés d'orgueil, et vous étiez un peuple de criminels. » Les commentateurs s'accordent à voir dans le fa' de « afalam » la réponse de « amma », le verbe « il leur sera dit » étant sous-entendu. Al-Zamakhshari et Abu Hayyan précisent qu'il faut comprendre : « Mes messagers ne sont-ils pas venus vous ? Et mes versets ne vous ont-ils pas été récités ? », l'élément coordonné étant omis. Al-Tabari et al-Sam'ani expliquent l'orgueil comme la recherche de la grandeur en refusant le monothéisme, et tout incroyant étant orgueilleux. Al-Qurtubi, al-Nasafi et Ibn Kathir entendent le « criminel » comme le mécréant, celui qui acquiert les péchés et l'incrédulité. Ibn 'Ashur note que l'expression « un peuple » indique que le crime est devenu chez eux un trait de caractère. Al-Razi relève aussi, contre les mu'tazilites, que la punition ne saurait être due qu'après la venue de la loi révélée. Le contexte relie ce verset à la scène du jugement où chaque communauté est appelée à son Livre, et il oppose le sort des croyants à celui des incroyants.

Ce verset décrit la réaction des mécréants lorsqu'on leur rappelle que la promesse d'Allah est vraie et que l'Heure est sans aucun doute à venir. Ils répondent qu'ils ne savent pas ce qu'est l'Heure, qu'ils n'en ont qu'une supposition, et qu'ils n'en sont pas certains. Les commentateurs expliquent cette réponse soit comme un déni de la résurrection et de la puissance divine de faire revivre les morts, soit comme une moquerie. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi et Ibn Kathir la lisent comme un rejet de la promesse divine, Ibn Kathir précisant qu'ils ne voient pas la survenue de l'Heure que comme une conjecture faible. Al-Razi distingue deux groupes parmi les infidèles : ceux qui nient catégoriquement la résurrection et ceux qui hésitent. Il considère que ce verset vise le second groupe, et il ajoute que ces derniers se moquaient en parlant ainsi. Ibn 'Ashur reprend cette lecture et y voit une raillerie. Ibn 'Atiyya, lui, explique que le sens est qu'ils conjecturent après avoir entendu le message, sans en tirer de certitude. Concernant la récitation, la majorité lit « wa-s-sa'atu » au nominatif, tandis que Hamza lit « wa-s-sa'ata » à l'accusatif. Al-Tabari juge les deux lectures correctes et de sens proche. Sur la construction grammaticale de l'expression « in nazunnu illa zannan », les avis divergent : al-Mubarrad la rétablit par inversion, certains y voient une proposition elliptique, Ibn Hisham un zann indéterminé, et Abu Hayyan la juge inacceptable. Le contexte du passage est celui du Jour du Jugement : les livres d'actes sont exhibés, les croyants entrent dans la miséricorde divine, et les incroyants sont réprimandés pour leur orgueil envers les versets.

Les commentateurs expliquent que, le Jour du Jugement, les mécréants verront apparaître les conséquences de leurs mauvaises actions, qu'ils tenaient pour peu graves, et que le châtiment dont ils se moquaient les enveloppera. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et al-Qurtubi précisent qu'il s'agit de voir la laideur de leurs œuvres lorsqu'ils liront les registres que les anges gardiens ont tenus. Al-Nasafi et al-Qurtubi relèvent que le mot « sayyi'at » peut désigner les châtiments eux-mêmes, à l'image du verset disant que la rétribution d'une mauvaise action est une mauvaise action semblable. Tous s'accordent à dire que le verbe « hâqa » ne s'emploie que pour un malheur. Pour le verset suivant, al-Dahhak explique que Dieu les abandonne dans le Feu comme ils ont abandonné Son ordre, Sa'id ibn Jubayr y voit l'abandon de tout bien, tandis qu'al-Razi propose deux sens : être laissés dans le tourment, ou être traités comme une chose oubliée que l'on néglige. Al-Razi souligne aussi que le moquerie ajoute à l'obstination dans le déni, ce qui rend ce groupe plus coupable que le premier. Ibn 'Ashur étend la moquerie à toutes les paroles où l'islam était tourné en dérision, comme les propos sur le doute et les menaces de biens dans l'au-delà. La plupart des commentateurs voient dans la préposition « bihi » une valeur de cause. Aucun jugement juridique n'est tiré de ces versets, et les variantes de lecture du mot « as-sâ'a » n'affectent guère le sens.

Les commentateurs expliquent que Dieu dit aux mécréants, au Jour de la Résurrection, qu'Il les abandonne au châtiment et ne les regardera plus avec miséricorde, comme eux-mêmes ont abandonné la foi et les œuvres en vue de la rencontre de ce jour. Leur demeure est le Feu, et personne ne viendra à leur secours. La plupart des exégètes s'accordent à donner au verbe « oublier » le sens d'« abandonner ». Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi et Abu al-Su'ud le comprennent ainsi : Dieu les laisse dans le Feu. Al-Baghawi précise qu'il s'agit de leur abandon de la foi et de l'action. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi et al-Shawkani y voient plutôt le fait de traiter les mécréants comme une chose oubliée, sans égard. Ibn Juzayy indique que le mot peut signifier l'abandon ou l'inattention, et al-Sha'rawi insiste sur l'absence de regard miséricordieux. Ibn 'Ashur note que l'oubli désigne ici un abandon éternel, car la mention de la demeure dans le Feu l'exprime. Le Zamakhshari et Abu Hayyan expliquent que l'expression « rencontre de ce jour » est une métonymie pour la rencontre avec Dieu et Sa rétribution. Plusieurs commentateurs, dont Ibn 'Ashur, soulignent que la kaf de « comme » marque la réciprocité : la rétribution est de même nature que l'acte. La plupart considèrent le passage comme une réprimande et un désespoir imposé aux mécréants.

Les commentateurs expliquent que ce verset annonce aux infidèles que le châtiment qui les frappe est la conséquence de leur attitude : ils ont tourné en dérision les signes d'Allah, c'est-à-dire le Coran et les preuves qu'Il a établies, et la vie d'ici-bas, avec ses ornements et ses plaisirs, les a trompés au point de croire qu'il n'y a ni résurrection ni reddition des comptes. Pour cette raison, ils ne sortiront pas du Feu et il ne leur sera pas demandé de réparer leur relation avec leur Seigneur, car le repentir ne leur servira à rien en ce jour-là. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et al-Baghawi s'accordent sur ce sens général, en précisant que la négation est absolue. Sur la lecture, Hamza et al-Kisa'i lisent « lā yakhrujūna » avec une voyelle d'ouverture sur le yā', tandis que la majorité lit « lā yukhrajūna », et Ibn 'Atiyya et Abu Hayyan notent que les deux lectures impliquent respectivement la sortie et l'expulsion. Le sens de « yusta'tabūn » est expliqué par al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi et Ibn Kathir comme le fait d'être agréés ou de voir Allah se satisfaire d'eux. Ibn al-Qayyim distingue ce type de demande de réconciliation, impossible dans l'au-delà, de celui qui est possible en ce monde. Le passage est souvent relié à la louange finale d'Allah, Seigneur des cieux, de la terre et des mondes, à qui appartient la grandeur, Lui qui est le Puissant et le Sage. Les commentateurs ne divergent pas sur le fond, seulement sur les détails lexicaux et les lectures.

Ce verset clôt la sourate en affirmant que la louange appartient à Dieu seul, car Il est le Seigneur des cieux, de la terre et de tous les mondes. Al-Tabari explique que cette louange est due à ses bienfaits envers ses créatures, et qu'elle lui revient et non aux idoles ni aux divinités que l'on adore en dehors de Lui. Ibn Kathir et al-Nasafi comprennent la seigneurie comme la propriété, la maîtrise et la gestion des cieux, de la terre et de ce qu'ils contiennent, tandis qu'Ibn Sa'di ajoute que sa seigneurie sur chaque créature, qu'il a créée et élevée, est la raison pour laquelle la louange lui est due à Lui seul. Al-Baghawi, al-Shawkani et al-Alusi soulignent que la répétition du mot Seigneur indique que sa seigneurie sur chacun de ces domaines est première et non empruntée. Ibn Atiyya et al-Qasimi voient dans le verset un rejet de l'idolâtrie et une affirmation de la divinité de Dieu. Ibn Ashur le relie à l'ensemble de la sourate, le présentant comme une conclusion qui loue Dieu pour les preuves, les avertissements et les bienfaits évoqués auparavant. Les lecteurs Mujahid, Humayd et Ibn Muhaysin ont lu le mot Seigneur au nominatif, signifiant Il est le Seigneur, alors que la majorité le lit au génitif comme attribut de Dieu, comme le rapportent al-Qurtubi et Abu Hayyan. Al-Razi note que le terme mondes englobe toute créature, corps et esprits. Les commentateurs s'accordent sur le sens apparent : Dieu seul mérite la louange parce qu'Il est le Seigneur de tout ce qui existe.

Ce verset clôt le passage en proclamant la grandeur de Dieu, après avoir annoncé que les damnés seront abandonnés et punis pour avoir raillé les signes divins et s'être laissé séduire par la vie d'ici-bas. Louange donc à Dieu, Seigneur des cieux, de la terre et des mondes, à Lui seul appartient la grandeur (al-kibriyâ') dans les cieux et sur la terre, et Il est le Puissant, le Sage. Presque tous les commentateurs, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi ou encore al-Jalalayn, entendent la grandeur comme la majesté, la gloire et l'autorité qui ne souffrent aucun rival. Al-Mawardi recense plusieurs sens possibles du mot : la grandeur, la souveraineté, la noblesse ou la permanence éternelle, et ce dernier sens est aussi relevé par al-Qurtubi, qui y ajoute la puissance et la perfection. Pour Ibn 'Atiyya et al-Zamakhshari, la louange exprime la reconnaissance de la seigneurie de Dieu et réfute le culte des idoles. Ibn 'Ashur voit dans la particule fa' une conséquence de tout ce qui précède dans la sourate, c'est-à-dire des bienfaits et des menaces divines. Plusieurs auteurs, dont al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir et al-Alusi, citent le hadith qualifié de sacré où Dieu dit que la grandeur est son manteau et la majesté son pagne, et qu'il châtie quiconque les lui dispute. Al-Shinqiti en tire l'idée que Dieu seul doit être adoré dans les cieux et sur la terre. Sur le sens des noms divins, les commentateurs s'accordent : al-'Aziz est le Tout-Puissant que nul ne peut vaincre, et al-Hakim est celui qui place chaque chose à sa juste place.
en: Most commentators hold that the disjointed letters « Ha Mim » at the opening belong to the ambiguous (mutashabih) matters that are to be believed without a detailed meaning. Ibn Kathir and al-Jaza'iri leave their meaning to God's knowledge, and al-Sha'rawi places them among the unseen (ghayb) that one believes in without exploring. For the next verse, « the revelation of the Book from God, the Mighty, the Wise », most identify the revelation with the Qur'an. Al-Tabari explains al-'Aziz as the one who punishes his enemies and al-Hakim as the one who directs the affairs of his creation. Ibn 'Atiyya understands might as a general strength shown both in severity and in protection, and wisdom as the perfect fitting of things. Al-Razi argues that it is more proper to attach these two attributes to God rather than to the Book, since the literal sense is preferable to the figurative. The sources agree the surah is Meccan, with the sole exception, according to Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada, of verse 14, which al-Mawardi and others connect with 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. The verses that follow, on the heavens and earth, human creation, the alternation of night and day, rain and winds, are read by the commentators as signs of God's oneness; al-Razi and Ibn Kathir note a gradation from believers to the certain to the people of reason. The readings differ: Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read « ayat » in the oblique case as a coordination, while the majority reads the nominative as a new clause. Al-Tabari judges both readings valid.

This verse states that the Book is a revelation sent down from Allah, the Mighty who avenges His enemies and the Wise in governing His creation. The commentators agree that the Book is the Qur'an and that the two names al-'Aziz and al-Hakim affirm the power and wisdom of its author. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi read the phrase as a plain statement that the Qur'an comes from God. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Nasafi discuss the grammar: the opening letters Ha Mim may serve as a subject with tanzil al-kitab as its predicate, or be taken as a mere list of letters. Al-Razi prefers linking the two attributes to God rather than to the Book, since this is the literal meaning and strengthens the proof that the Qur'an is true. Abu Hayyan argues that linking them to the Book is not acceptable grammatically here. Al-Mawardi notes two senses of the wording: the Book opens with God's name as an author begins his work, and the phrase magnifies the Book's rank. Ibn 'Ashur observes that the construction draws the listener's attention and asserts a fact that no one would dispute. The differences therefore concern mainly grammar and rhetoric rather than the core meaning.

The commentators explain that the verse states that in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and in everything they contain, there are clear signs and proofs of God's oneness and power, and that only believers who reflect upon them benefit from them. Al-Tabari says that the heaven from which rain falls and the earth from which creatures emerge are proofs and arguments for those who believe when they consider and see them. Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and Ibn Ashur agree that the verse draws attention to the signs of the outer universe, and that faith is what prepares the heart to benefit from them.

Al-Razi and al-Jaza'iri hold that the heavens and the earth are not themselves the sign, but their creation is, since it shows the existence of a Creator who chooses. Al-Shinqiti notes that these signs are explained in many other verses of the Qur'an. Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir observe that the signs are mentioned in general terms, without detail, which stirs reflection; the reason they are assigned to believers is that faith includes reason and affirmation.

The readers differ on the case of the word 'ayat' that follows. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read it in the accusative, coordinated with the earlier 'la-ayat', while the others read it in the nominative as an independent clause. Al-Tabari and al-Farra' justify the genitive by reference to what precedes, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya find the nominative more correct, with the preposition understood. Abu Hayyan treats coordination under two governing elements as a question with four positions.

The commentators agree that the signs mentioned afterwards, such as the creation of human beings and animals, the alternation of night and day, and rain and winds, form three progressive levels: faith, certainty, then reason, as Ibn Kathir and al-Razi observe.

The commentators explain that this verse directs attention to God's signs in the creation of human beings and in the living creatures that spread across the earth. These are proofs and evidence of the Creator's power and oneness, for a people who have certainty, meaning those who believe in the truth with knowledge and conviction. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand creation to include the stages of human development, from a drop of fluid to a clinging clot and then a lump of flesh, until a complete human being is formed. The word for spreading refers to scattering and multiplication, and "creature" means anything that crawls or walks on the earth apart from humankind. The exegetes agree that these signs are addressed to the one who reflects and keeps reflecting, and that certainty is a higher rank than faith in this context, as Ibn Kathir notes when he traces the progression from faith to certainty to reason across the following verses.

On the recitation, the readers differed. Most readers of Medina, Basra and some of Kufa read "āyātun" in the nominative, as a new beginning or a resumption, while Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read "āyātin" in the genitive, linking it to the subject of "inna" or to what precedes. Al-Tabari judges both readings valid and sound in meaning. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan observe that coordinating two governed items under two different governors is debated among grammarians, and that Sibawayh explained this reading by implying the preposition. Al-Razi holds that the signs are specific to believers, since they alone benefit from them, whereas the Mu'tazilites consider them general to both believer and unbeliever. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Razi clarify that the address is aimed at the polytheists, and that their failure to benefit explains the emphatic wording.

In sum, the verse invites reflection on both the heavens, the earth and the creatures, and the fruit of such reflection is certainty in God and in what He has revealed.

The commentators read this verse as a call to reflect on God's signs in the created order: the alternation of night and day, the rain sent down from the sky, which is called provision because it is the cause of sustenance, and by which the dead earth is brought to life, and the turning of the winds. They agree that these phenomena are proofs of God's power and oneness for people who reason. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the winds change direction and character, from north to south, from gentle breezes to storms, and al-Tabari, citing Qatada, adds that God makes them a mercy at times and a punishment at others. Al-Mawardi offers two readings of the provision: the rain itself, or what God has decreed in the heavens as the livelihood of His servants. Ibn 'Atiyya understands the alternation of night and day either as light and darkness or as one following the other. Al-Razi draws several arguments for a choosing Creator from the formation of clouds, the growth of plants and the variety of their kinds, and compares this verse with al-Baqara 2:164. Al-Zamakhshari describes how sincere people who look at the heavens and the earth, then at themselves and at the constantly renewed events, move from faith to certainty and then to firmly established understanding. The readers differ on the case of the word for signs: Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it in the genitive, while the others read it in the nominative. There is also a grammatical debate: al-Akhfash and many Kufans allow coordination after two different governing words, while Sibawayh and most Basrans reject it. Modern commentators such as Ibn Sa'di and al-Jaza'iri take the verse as evidence of God's lordship, divinity and the resurrection.

This verse states that the signs of God recited to the Prophet ﷺ are true proofs, free of falsehood, and that whoever does not believe in them will find no later account worth believing. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that if the polytheists do not believe in this Qur'an and the proofs of God's oneness it contains, then in what speech will they believe after God's word and His signs? Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan read this as a rebuke and reproach, with the Qur'an itself as the referent. Al-Baghawi, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari note that “after God and His signs” may mean “after the signs of God”, the divine name being mentioned to magnify them, like the phrase “Zayd pleased me and his generosity”. Ibn 'Atiyya holds that a word must be understood, namely reciting the matter of these signs and the lesson in them, though he allows that the signs may mean the Qur'an itself. All agree that the question is rhetorical and carries the sense of a denial. The readings differ: most read “yu'minun” in the third person, while Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr read “tu'minun” in the second person. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari note that the plural second person fits “wa fi khalqikum”, and al-Tabari prefers the third person because it follows the preceding verses. Al-Razi also observes that the verse shows knowledge of these signs comes through reason rather than transmission alone, and that rejecting belief after such signs calls for careful reflection on the proofs of the religion.

This verse announces a severe punishment and ruin, which the commentators describe either as a valley in hell or as a formula of warning, for every great liar who commits many sins. The commentators agree that the affak is the one who lies greatly and that the athim is the one who is intensely engaged in sin, both intensive forms pointing to repeated lying and wrongdoing. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read the verse within its context of God's signs in the heavens and the earth and of the refusal of those who do not believe after they appear. Al-Qurtubi, al-Nasafi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Mahalli with al-Suyuti limit themselves to explaining the words in their ordinary meanings. Al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan report that persistence in disbelief and arrogance when the Quran is heard are among this sinner's traits. Al-Zamakhshari holds that thumma here signals surprise, meaning that persisting after hearing such clear signs is remarkable. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya consider the verse to address anyone who harms God's religion, though most commentators name an-Nadr ibn al-Harith or Abu Jahl as the occasion of revelation. Ibn 'Atiyya states that the verse applies to everyone who meets these descriptions until the Day of Resurrection. Al-Tabari leans toward the third-person reading of the following verse because of its context, while judging both readings valid. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the persistent arrogance upon hearing the Quran drives its holder to repeated denial and sin, and that the word 'alima here means to hear. Al-Shawkani, al-Jaza'iri and Ibn Sa'di describe this punishment as painful and humiliating, among the most severe.

This verse describes the person who constantly lies and commits sin, and who, when the verses of God are recited to him, persists in disbelief with arrogance, as though he had never heard them. He is then given the news of a painful punishment. The commentators explain that "affak" means the great liar, with Ibn Jurayj taking it to mean one who denies his Lord and Qatada taking it to mean the soothsayer, while "athim" denotes one who greatly commits sins. Al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and others explain that persistence (al-israr) means remaining steadfast in disbelief; al-Mawardi also reports the view of Ibn 'Isa that the word derives from tying a purse, that is, a firm resolve of the heart. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan, al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy read the particle "thumma" (then) as indicating a gap in rank: persisting after hearing such verses is considered strange by reason and by nature. They also agree that arrogance means scorning the verses and being self-satisfied. Several, including Ibn 'Abbas, link the occasion of revelation to al-Nadr ibn al-Harith or Abu Jahl, while Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi hold that the verse applies to everyone who shows these traits. Mocking the verses is presented as the next stage of this attitude. The word "bashshir" is used ironically. The verse adds that Hell awaits such people, that their wealth and their false gods will not avail them, and that they will suffer a humiliating and great punishment.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the habitual liar and sinner who, when he hears any part of Allah's signs, that is the Qur'an, or learns that something belongs to them, mocks it, and so receives a punishment that humiliates him. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi understand it as referring to one who hears the Qur'an and then persists in disbelief out of arrogance. Al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud note that the mockery may extend to all the verses, not only the one he heard. Al-Tabari and al-Wahidi report that it was revealed concerning Abu Jahl or al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, but Ibn 'Atiyya holds that its meaning is general and applies to anyone with this description until the Day of Judgment, an opinion also held by al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur. On the phrase 'from behind them', Ibn Abbas, al-Qurtubi and al-Jalalayn take it to mean 'before them', while others understand it as what comes after their deeds. The pronoun in 'took them' refers to the signs, though it may also refer to 'something', as al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan note. On recitation, Ibn Kathir and Hafs read 'painful' as an adjective of 'punishment', while the others attach it to 'filth', which Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi consider the severest torment. Al-Razi distinguishes the painful punishment that afflicts the body from the humiliating one that wounds dignity. The commentators agree that the humiliation answers the arrogance of these people, and they do not specify a number of individuals meant.

The commentators explain that the words 'behind them is Hell' mean that Hell awaits these mockers of God's signs, and they differ on the meaning of the word 'wara'' (behind). Ibn 'Abbas, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most scholars take it to mean 'in front of them', that Hell lies ahead of them and they will reach it, while others understand it as 'behind'. Az-Zamakhshari notes that the word denotes the direction that hides a person, whether behind or ahead. The commentators state that neither wealth, nor children, nor the idols and leaders they had taken as allies will avail them that day, and that they will suffer a great punishment, which the Qur'an also calls humiliating. Al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report that the verse was revealed about al-Nadr ibn al-Harith or Abu Jahl, whereas al-Mawardi and Ibn 'Atiyya hold that it applies to anyone with these same traits until the Day of Judgment. Al-Kalbi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Sa'di understand 'wara'' as what comes after the end of life, so the punishment belongs to the afterlife. Ibn 'Ashur sees in the phrase a picture of the nearness of punishment and the heedlessness of those who face it. Al-Shinqiti and al-Sha'rawi argue that 'wara'' here means 'in front', supporting this with examples from Arabic. Al-Alusi combines both meanings: Hell is ahead of them because they are heading toward it, or behind them because they turn away from it. The commentators agree that the great and humiliating punishment refers to the torment of the Last Day, and most attribute it to their rejection of the signs and their mockery of them.

The commentators explain that "This is guidance" refers to the Qur'an, which is a clear proof and a light that leads to the truth and the straight path. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi observe that the word "guidance" here reaches the highest degree of perfection, to the point that it is almost guidance itself, much as one says "Zayd is a man" meaning he is complete in manhood. As for those who disbelieved in the signs of their Lord, meaning those who denied the Qur'anic proofs and neither believed in nor acted upon them, they will receive a painful punishment. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi agree that "rijz" means the most severe punishment or a painful torment. They differ on the reading: Ibn Kathir and Hafs read "alimun" in the nominative, as an adjective of the punishment, while the other readers read it in the genitive, as an adjective of "rijz". Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi note that "rijz" may also mean filth or impurity, as in the verse about pus-like water, so the punishment would be drinking an impure draught. Ibn Ashur and al-Shinqiti point out that the apparent repetition is not a true one, since punishment comes in several kinds, and that "min" may mark explanation or partition. The commentators do not disagree on the general sense of the verse, but on its grammatical construction and on the nuance of the word "rijz".

This verse states that God subjected the sea to you so that ships sail on it by His command, so that you may seek His bounty, and so that you may be grateful. The commentators explain that sailing happens by God's permission and power, since He made the sea's surface smooth and able to carry wood while not preventing diving. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi, al-Jalalayn and the Muyassar tafsir agree that seeking His bounty mainly means trade and earning a livelihood. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi, Abu Hayyan and Abu al-Su'ud add diving for pearls and coral, extracting fresh meat, and hunting. Ibn 'Atiyya includes pilgrimage and jihad among the forms of seeking bounty, and Ibn 'Ashur adds travel to visit family and for recreation. Al-Jaza'iri understands it as travelling from region to region to seek sustenance. Al-Sam'ani, quoting Ibn 'Uyayna, holds that gratitude is obligatory for every Muslim, because God linked provision to thankfulness. Al-Sha'rawi recommends praising God whenever one sees a sign of His blessings and cites the supplication for boarding a ship. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di stress that the blessing comes from God alone, and that gratitude means worshipping Him and obeying Him. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi also note variant readings of the word minhu in the following verse, which concern grammar more than meaning.

This verse says that God subjected to human beings everything in the heavens and on the earth, including the sun, the moon, the stars, animals, trees, mountains, rivers and ships, for their benefit and welfare. The commentators agree that the phrase "all of it from Him" means that all these blessings come from God alone, through His grace and generosity, and that no partner shares in their creation or in their being made subservient, which calls for gratitude and monotheism. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir relate from Ibn 'Abbas that everything comes from God, and that no disputer can deny this. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan examine the grammar of the word "minhu": it may be a circumstantial phrase, or the predicate of an omitted subject, and the meaning would be that God first brought these things into existence and then subjected them to His creatures. Some readers recited "minnatan" in the accusative as a verbal noun, or "minnuhu" with a different vowelling; Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan report these readings and note that some of their chains of transmission are weak. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and al-Alusi set out the various possibilities without choosing between them. All stress that the signs are meant for those who reflect, that is, who use their reason to contemplate creation.

This verse tells the believers to forgive those who do not hope for the Days of God, meaning those who do not expect His decisive days against their enemies and do not fear His punishment, bearing their harm without repaying it in kind. The commentators read Dayy Allah as His victories and punishments against nations, and some as the rewards He set for the believers. God, they explain, will recompense those people for what they have earned of sin and harm, so the believers need not avenge themselves. Most agree that the forgiveness meant is leaving aside retaliation for verbal and personal insults. The main disagreement is whether the verse was abrogated. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Atiyya, hold it abrogated by the verses on fighting, citing Qatada, al-Dahhak and Abu Salih. Others, such as Ibn Juzayy, Ibn 'Ashur and al-Alusi, consider it not abrogated, since forgiving harm is always praiseworthy or because it concerns only minor disputes. The occasion of revelation is also debated. Al-Mawardi and al-Baghawi relate it to 'Umar, who wanted to strike a man who had insulted him, while al-Samani, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Razi relate it to the well of al-Muraysi' and Abd Allah ibn Ubayy. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Qurtubi regard these reports as weak and see the verse as Meccan, addressing persecuted Muslims. On recitation, the majority read the verb with ya and Allah as subject, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with nun of majesty, and the passive reading attributed to Abu Ja'far was judged a solecism by Abu 'Amr. The verse closes by stating that each person is repaid according to his deeds, the good for himself and the evil against himself, before the return to God.

The commentators explain that this verse states a general principle: whoever does good benefits himself, and whoever does evil bears its burden alone, and then all of you will be returned to your Lord, who will repay you. Al-Tabari explains that the one who obeys God seeks only to free his own soul from God's punishment, that God is independent of His servants' deeds, and that the wrongdoer harms no one but himself. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di likewise stress that reward and punishment follow each person's own deeds.

Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud focus on the prepositions: the lam in "for himself" signals benefit and advantage, while "against it" in the second half signals harm. Ibn 'Atiyya adds that this choice of wording expresses gains and losses, and that returning to God means returning to His judgment.

The verse follows directly after an instruction to believers to forgive those who do not hope for the Days of God. Al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that many exegetes regard that instruction as abrogated by the verses on fighting, while Ibn 'Atiyya understands it as a call to avoid disputes over trivial matters. Ibn 'Ashur finds several reports on the occasion of revelation weak and prefers the context of Mecca, where the Muslims had to endure insults.

The commentators agree on the general meaning of the verse. Their disagreements concern how it connects to the preceding verses and whether the earlier command it follows was abrogated.

God recounts the favours He bestowed on the Children of Israel: He gave them the Book, which most commentators take to be the Torah, wisdom and understanding of the Book along with judgment between people, and prophethood, since many prophets arose among them. He provided them with good, lawful provision such as manna and quails, and preferred them over the peoples of their time. Ibn 'Abbas says that no one in their era was more honoured by God. Al-Tabari takes the Book to include both the Torah and the Gospel, and understanding to mean knowledge of the sunnas that are not in the Book. The clear signs of the matter are read by some as miracles and decisive proofs, by al-Sudi as the explanation of what is lawful and unlawful, and by others as evidence of the mission of Muhammad ﷺ. Al-Nahhas, cited by Ibn al-Jawzi, places the disagreement after Yusha ibn Nun, when some believed and others disbelieved. The exegetes agree that the disagreement came after knowledge had arrived, out of rebellion, envy and the pursuit of leadership. Al-Zamakhshari also mentions enmity and jealousy. Ibn Kathir sees in the passage a warning to this community not to follow their path. The phrase placing you on a way of the affair is explained by Ibn Zayd as religion, by Qatada as obligations and rulings, by Muqatil as clear proof, and by al-Kalbi as the prophetic custom. Al-Sha'rawi notes that the number of prophets among them was not a merit but a sign of their corruption, while Ibn 'Ashur reads the passage as consolation for the Prophet facing his people. Al-Shinqiti stresses that the community of Muhammad ﷺ is the best of nations, and that the preference given to the Children of Israel refers to their earlier time.

This verse says that God gave the Children of Israel clear proofs in matters of religion, and that they only disagreed after knowledge had come to them, out of envy among themselves. The commentators differ on what the "clear proofs of the matter" are. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sudi, al-Nasafi, Ibn Kathir and others take them to be the clear rulings on the lawful and the unlawful in the Torah, while Ibn 'Abbas in another report, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur take them to be knowledge of the Prophet Muhammad's mission and the signs of his prophethood. Most agree that the "baghy" (unjust rivalry) was envy, hostility and the pursuit of leadership. Al-Dahhak understood it as defiance of the Prophet ﷺ by denying what was in their scriptures, and Yahya ibn Adam held that they altered their Book out of attachment to worldly gain. Al-Mawardi reports that the disagreement began after Yusha' ibn Nun, and al-Qurtubi that it began after the Prophet's mission. All agree that God will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning what they disputed. Ibn Kathir and al-Muntakhab see in the verse a warning to this community not to follow their path, while al-Tabari does not develop this point. Ibn Kathir and al-Jalalayn also read the verse as a comfort to the Prophet ﷺ and an introduction to the next verse about the path set for him.

The commentators explain that, after recounting the favours given to the Children of Israel, God addresses His Prophet ﷺ: He has placed him upon a clear path, a sharia of the command, which he must follow without yielding to the desires of those who do not know. Most agree that the word sharia here means religion, path, and creed. Others specify its content: al-Tabari and Ibn Abbas link it to the path of guidance; Qatada to obligations, prescribed limits, and commands and prohibitions; Muqatil to clear evidence; al-Kalbi to the prophetic practice; and Ibn Zayd to religion as the way to salvation. Al-Sam'ani and al-Mawardi report similar views, and al-Zamakhshari takes it as the firm law established by proofs.

Regarding those who do not know, the majority identify them as the pagans of Quraysh who urged the Prophet to return to the religion of his forefathers, a context reported by al-Baghawi and al-Razi. Other commentators such as Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi also mention the Jews of Qurayza and al-Nadir. All agree that following their desires would bring ruin, that these people cannot shield the Prophet from God's punishment, that the wrongdoers support one another, and that God is the protector of the righteous. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari stress the contrast between God's guardianship and the mutual alliances of the unjust.

Ibn Ashur notes that the word "then" marks a rank above what was given to the Children of Israel, and that the prohibition, though addressed to the Prophet, is meant for his community, a view also developed by al-Shinqiti. Ibn al-Arabi, quoted by al-Qurtubi, adds that this verse does not prove that earlier law is not binding on us, since the dispute concerns what the Prophet related about earlier law in a context of praise.

This verse tells the Prophet ﷺ that God has placed him on a clear path of the religion, so he must follow it and not the desires of those who do not know God, because they cannot spare him anything of God's punishment if he follows them. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir explain that the wrongdoers here are the polytheists, who support one another, while God is the ally of the righteous, those who guard themselves against polytheism and sins. As for the word shari'a, the commentators offer closely related meanings: Qatada takes it to be the obligations, the prescribed limits and the commands and prohibitions; Ibn Zayd takes it to be the religion; Muqatil takes it to be the clear proof, since it leads to the truth; al-Kalbi takes it to be the sunna, since the Prophet follows the path of the prophets before him. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari describe it as a way that leads people to God. All agree in identifying the ignorant with the leaders of Quraysh, who urged him to return to the religion of his forefathers. Al-Zamakhshari stresses the sharp contrast between the two loyalties. Ibn 'Ashur explains that not avail here means not to ward off punishment, and that the verse gives the reason for forbidding the following of their desires. The scholars differ mainly over the precise meaning of shari'a and the identity of the ignorant, without changing the general sense of the verse.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the Qur'an as insights for mankind, meaning evidence by which people distinguish truth from falsehood and recognise the path of right guidance. It is also a guidance away from error and a mercy that spares from punishment, yet its full benefit belongs to those who have certainty, that is, who firmly believe in its truth and that it is a revelation from the Mighty, the Wise. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand these insights as proofs and landmarks concerning the laws and their limits, whereas al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi take them as insights of the heart. Ibn Zayd adds that the sight and hearing meant here belong to the heart and not to worldly perception.

The verse continues with a rebuke of those who commit evil deeds and suppose they will be treated like the believers. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi agree that life and death apply to both groups, the believer remaining a believer in life and death and the disbeliever remaining a disbeliever, as reported from Mujahid and al-Layth. The disagreement concerns the reading of the word sawa'. The readers of Medina and Basra read it in the nominative, while Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read it in the accusative; Abu Ubayd preferred the accusative, and al-Tabari judged both readings valid and sound in meaning.

Some grammarians cited by al-Tabari held that life and death refer only to the disbelievers, so that their condition in both states is evil, while others extended them to both groups, and Ibn Atiyya found both readings plausible. Several pious figures, such as al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym and al-Fudayl ibn Iyad, repeated this verse in tears through the night, so that it came to be called the weeping of the worshippers.

This verse is a rebuke: God rejects the assumption of those who have committed evil deeds, namely associating partners with God and sinning, that He will treat them in life and in death as He treats those who believe and do righteous deeds. Commentators such as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi agree that this assumption is wrong and that the judgment it implies is evil, and they agree that the outcome for the two groups is clearly different.

The main disagreement concerns what equality in life and death means. Mujahid, Qatada, al-Kalbi and al-Baghawi take it that the believer remains a believer in this world and the next, and the disbeliever remains a disbeliever, each being raised as he died. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi, by contrast, take the equality to concern worldly conditions such as health and provision, which may resemble each other, with the difference appearing at death; al-Razi also mentions that the denial may concern equality at death after equality in life.

Readers also differ on the case of the word sawa'. Most read it in the nominative, while Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read it in the accusative, a reading Abu 'Ubayd preferred. The grammarians discuss how the clause following it should be parsed.

According to Mujahid, Ibn 'Abbas and al-Kalbi, the verse refers to certain Meccan notables. Widely cited is the report that Tamim al-Dari repeated it through the night in tears, and the verse came to be called the weeping of the worshippers.

This part of the verse states that God created the heavens and the earth with truth, meaning with justice and wisdom and not in vain, so that every soul may be repaid for what it has earned, good or bad, and no one is wronged in that repayment. Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan take the lam of «wa-li-tujza» as linked to «bil-haqq», since it carries the sense of purpose: creation serves to establish justice. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Razi attach it instead to an implied purpose, namely that God might show through them His power. Ibn Atiyya also allows that this lam may express outcome: some were guided by the creation and others strayed from it, so that each is repaid according to his deeds. As for «wa-hum la yuzlamun», al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain it as meaning that nothing of their due is diminished, while al-Alusi and Abu al-Su'ud hold that the word «wronged» is used only to affirm God's absolute freedom from injustice, since He cannot commit it. Ibn 'Ashur links the passage to the idea that justice requires a distinction between the doer of good and the doer of evil, and that judgment must therefore take place after death. The commentators agree that the verse rules out equating the believer with the disbeliever and that full recompense is not completed in this world alone. Other exegetes simply explain «haqq» as what is established and firm.

The verse describes the one who takes his own desire as his god, following only what he himself wishes. God has led him astray knowingly, sealed his hearing and heart, and covered his sight, so that none can guide him after God; the verse then calls on the reader to reflect. Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatada explain that this disbeliever makes his religion whatever he desires, never refraining from anything and not fearing God, while Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrima and Muqatil understand that he worships what his desire finds appealing, like the Quraysh who worshipped stones and discarded them for better ones; al-Tabari adopts this second reading as the most evident in context. On the phrase "led astray knowingly", most commentators such as Ibn Kathir take it as God's prior knowledge, Zamakhshari reads it as abandonment despite the man's awareness, and Razi relates it to the disposition of souls. The commentators agree that the Qur'an and the cited hadiths condemn desire that overrules reason, and several draw from this a rule of conduct. In context, the following verses report the disbelievers' denial of the Last Day, who say that only time destroys them; Ibn Kathir and others note that they speak from conjecture rather than knowledge, and that time should not be cursed, since God is its author.

God relates the words of those who deny resurrection: there is only this worldly life, in which some die and others live, and nothing follows. Commentators differ on the meaning of "we die and we live". Al-Kalbi and al-Baghawi take it as the death of parents and the life of children, al-Zamakhshari as some dying while others live, and al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Nasafi allow an inverted order, "we live and then die", a reading attributed to Ibn Mas'ud. Al-Razi suggests a reference to the state of being sperm in the loins before life. As for "only time destroys us", Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada explain it as the passing of days and nights and the length of life, Qatada adding the sense of age, Qutrub taking it as death, and 'Ikrima as God. All agree it denies the hereafter and is held on conjecture rather than knowledge. Several, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi, cite the hadith "Do not revile time, for God is Time" and explain that the true agent is God, to whom the blame returns. Ibn al-Jawzi adds that God is the one who destroys, not the time they imagine. The commentators agree that God answers that they have no sound knowledge, and that their only argument, demanding the return of their ancestors, is met by the reply that God gives life and causes death, then gathers mankind for the Day of Resurrection, about which there is no doubt.

This verse describes the stance of those who deny resurrection. When clear verses about the Hour are recited to them, their only reply is to tell the Prophet: bring back our fathers who have died, if you are truthful. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that calling this an argument is sarcastic, since it is no argument at all, and that the sense is that they have no proof whatsoever. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Sa'di tie their position to doubt and conjecture, and several note that for some it went together with denying the Creator and attributing life and death to time (al-dahr). Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi read God's reply as affirming that He gives life and death and then gathers people on the Day of Resurrection; whoever creates at the beginning can recreate. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi add that human beings pass through stages, from dust to a drop of semen, which shows the power to bring them back.

The scholars differ on several points. Al-Mawardi and Ibn Juzayy give different readings of "we die and we live": some die while others live, parents die while children live, or the order of the words is reversed. Al-Razi also observes that the objection is weak, since what does not occur now is not thereby impossible, just as we did not exist before we were born. Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi discuss the grammar of "hujjatahum" and the reading with nasb or raf', noting the various opinions. Ibn 'Ashur concludes that this speech is a way of evading clear proof and turning to obstinacy.

This passage answers the Meccan deniers of resurrection, who said that life is only this worldly life, that we die and live through the passing of time, and who demanded that their forefathers be brought back as proof. The commentators explain that the verse "Say: Allah gives you life, then causes you to die, then will gather you on the Day of Resurrection, about which there is no doubt" means that it is Allah, not time, who gives life and causes death. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read it as affirming that the One who originated creation can recreate, and that the gathering is for reward. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan present it as an argument from their own admissions: they accept that Allah gives life and death, and whoever can do that can also bring back their ancestors. The scholars differ on the meaning of "ad-dahr": Mujahid takes it as time, Qatada as the span of life, Qutrub as death, and Ikrima as Allah himself. Ibn Kathir cites the hadith "Do not revile time, for Allah is time," explaining that what is attributed to time returns to Allah. Several commentators, including al-Razi and al-Baghawi, note that most people do not know because they neglect reflection on the signs, and that their doubt arises from this neglect rather than from any real uncertainty about the Resurrection.

This verse states that dominion over the heavens and the earth belongs to God alone, and that on the day the Hour is established, those who uphold falsehood will be the losers. Al-Tabari explains that the falsehood meant is the claim of partners to God and the worship of other gods, and that the loss is that the righteous take the places in Paradise that the wrongdoers would have had, while the wrongdoers receive the places of the Fire. Ibn Kathir identifies them as the disbelievers who reject God's clear signs, and Ibn 'Atiyya links the verse to the Quraysh who demanded that their ancestors be brought back to life. The commentators agree on the general sense of a clear loss on the Day of Judgment. They differ on grammar: al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Qurtubi explain that the verb "yakhsaru" governs the time clause, with "yawma'idhin" as an apposition or emphasis, while others make the time depend on the sense of sovereignty. The following verses, which many commentators connect to this one, describe every community kneeling and summoned to its book. Al-Mawardi lists several meanings of "jathiya" (crouching, gathered, humbled), while al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi mainly retain the sense of kneeling. As for the book, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take it as the record of deeds, whereas Ibn 'Ashur takes it as the revealed law of each community. Al-Qasimi and Ibn Sa'di also note that the book may mean either sense.

This verse depicts the Day of Judgment, when every nation is seen kneeling in fear and awaiting its reckoning. The commentators agree that jathiya expresses the posture of one who is humbled and frightened. Mujahid, Qatada, al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd take it to mean kneeling, some specifying the crouching position of one ready to rise, and Ibn Abbas understands it as gathered together, 'Ikrima as distinct, and Mu'arrij, citing the dialect of Quraysh, as submissive. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya note that the verb jadhw is even more forceful than jathw. Al-Qurtubi and al-Baghawi report Salman al-Farisi's account that during one terrible period of that day people fall to their knees, even Abraham.

On the phrase "each nation is called to its book", the views differ. Ibn Abbas and Abu Salih take it as the record of deeds, good and bad, while Qatada and Mujahid link it to what the angels wrote down. Al-Sha'bi, al-Farra' and Ibn Qutayba understand it as the reckoning, and Yahya ibn Sallam holds that it refers to the scripture revealed to each nation, so that it may be examined on whether it was followed, a view Ibn Jarir also includes. Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Sa'di accept both meanings, and Ibn 'Ashur notes that the indefinite singular supports the sense of revealed scriptures. Al-Razi, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud mainly retain the record of deeds.

As for "istinsakh", most commentators, including Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi, understand that God commands the angels to record the deeds, some adding that they copy what is in the Preserved Tablet. Ibn Abbas, quoted by Ibn Kathir and al-Alusi, argues for this sense by saying that copying presupposes an original. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur discuss the precise meaning of nasakh, some seeing it as simple writing and others as reproducing from a model.

This verse belongs to the description of the Day of Judgment. Every community is seen kneeling and called to its book, and that book declares, in truth, that it records what people did. Most commentators agree that the book is the record of deeds, and they understand that it speaks against people because it shows exactly what was done, with nothing added or omitted. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi identify it with the register kept by the guardian angels, and al-Tabari reports from Ibn Abbas that it holds the deeds of the children of Adam. Other scholars name a different book. Mujahid and Muqatil, as cited by al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi, take it to be the Preserved Tablet, which bears witness to each person's fate, while Ibn Qutayba takes it to be the Quran, which reminds people of their deeds. Ibn Juzayy prefers the first view. The word nastansikh is explained in several ways. Ibn Abbas, al-Tabari, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir report that the angels copy from an original, either the Preserved Tablet or the Mother of the Book, and then compare the guardians' records with that copy, Ibn Abbas arguing that copying always requires a source. Al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi add that the record sheets are raised up and only those deeds that merit reward or punishment are kept. Al-Dahhak takes the verb to mean establishing, al-Suddi writing, and al-Hasan preserving. Ibn al-Qayyim suggests both senses may be intended, while al-Nasafi understands it simply as writing down, without copying from a source.

This verse describes the fate of the believers who did righteous deeds on the Day of Resurrection: their Lord will admit them into His mercy. Most commentators, including Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Nasafi, understand this mercy to mean Paradise, and Ibn Kathir supports this with the hadith in which God tells Paradise, 'You are My mercy'. Al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that the believers are those who affirmed God's oneness, obeyed His commands and refrained from what He forbade, and that entering His mercy means attaining what they strove for in this life. Abu al-Su'ud and al-Shawkani see this admission as a detail of what happens to the nations after they were addressed with the promise and the threat. All agree that the 'manifest triumph' is a clear success beyond which there is no further success. Al-Biqa'i adds that it is clear because it is unmixed with any turbulence, unlike the successes of this world, which remained obscure to those without certainty. Al-Razi distinguishes faith from righteous deeds, treating the latter as an additional element beyond faith, and notes that the Mu'tazilites read the condition for entry differently. He also observes that the word 'mercy' implies the reward is not owed. Al-Sa'di and Ibn 'Ashur explain that 'entering His mercy' covers every kind of blessing the soul can imagine, the mercy being presented as a place one enters. The passage belongs to the context of judgement and recompense on the Day of Resurrection.

This verse describes the fate of the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection. They will be told, as a rebuke and reproach, "Were My verses not recited to you? But you were arrogant, and you were a people of criminals." The commentators agree that the fa' in "afalam" answers the conditional particle "amma", with the verb "it will be said to them" understood. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan explain that the sense is: "Did My messengers not come to you, and were My verses not recited to you?", the first clause being omitted. Al-Tabari and al-Sam'ani understand arrogance as seeking greatness by rejecting monotheism, and they note that every disbeliever is arrogant. Al-Qurtubi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir take "criminals" to mean disbelievers who earn sins and unbelief. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the word "a people" shows that crime had become a trait of their character. Al-Razi adds, against the Mu'tazilites, that punishment is due only after the law has come. The verse belongs to the scene of judgement that begins with each community being called to its Book, and it sets the fate of the disbelievers against that of the believers.

This verse describes how the disbelievers respond when told that Allah's promise is true and that the Hour is undoubtedly coming. They say they do not know what the Hour is, that they only suppose it, and that they are not certain of it. The commentators read this reply either as a denial of resurrection and of God's power to bring the dead back, or as mockery. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir take it as a rejection of God's promise, with Ibn Kathir stressing that they regard the Hour's occurrence only as a weak conjecture. Al-Razi distinguishes two groups among the unbelievers: those who categorically deny resurrection and those who are doubtful and perplexed. He holds that this verse concerns the second group, and adds that they spoke in mockery. Ibn 'Ashur follows this reading and also sees derision in the reply. Ibn 'Atiyya explains that they conjecture only after hearing the message and that such conjecture gives no certainty. On recitation, most readers have the nominative 'wa-s-sa'atu', while Hamza reads the accusative 'wa-s-sa'ata', linking it to Allah's promise. Al-Tabari judges both readings sound and close in meaning. On the grammar of 'in nazunnu illa zannan', opinions differ: al-Mubarrad proposes a reversal of the clause, others an implied complement, and Abu Hayyan rejects several of these solutions. The surrounding passage concerns the Day of Judgment, when every community is summoned to its book, the believers enter God's mercy, and the disbelievers are reproached for their arrogance toward God's signs.

The commentators explain that on the Day of Judgment the disbelievers will see the evil consequences of their deeds, which they had considered minor, and the punishment they used to mock will surround them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi say the meaning is that the ugliness of their deeds will become clear when they read the records kept by the guardian angels, while al-Nasafi and al-Qurtubi note that "evil deeds" may mean their punishments, as in the verse that the recompense of an evil deed is an evil like it. All agree that the verb "haqa" is used only for something harmful. For the next verse, al-Dahhak explains that God leaves them in the Fire as they left His command, Sa'id ibn Jubayr takes it as being left without any good, and al-Razi offers two readings: being left in torment, or being treated as a forgotten thing that no one cares about. Al-Razi also argues that mockery added to their stubborn denial, making this group worse than the first. Ibn 'Ashur extends the mockery to every statement that ridiculed Islam, such as their words expressing doubt and their claims of wealth in the hereafter. Most commentators read the particle "bihi" as indicating cause. No legal ruling is drawn from these verses, and the differing recitations of "al-sa'a" do not change the meaning much.

The commentators explain that on the Day of Resurrection God tells the disbelievers that He will leave them to the punishment and will no longer regard them with mercy, just as they abandoned faith and good deeds in preparation for the meeting with this Day. Their abode is the Fire, and they have no helpers. Most exegetes agree that the word translated as forgetting here means abandoning. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and Abu al-Su'ud understand it this way: God leaves them in the Fire, and al-Baghawi specifies that they abandoned faith and action. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Shawkani read it rather as treating them like a forgotten thing that is no longer cared for. Ibn Juzayy notes that the word may mean either abandonment or inattention, while al-Sha'rawi stresses the withdrawal of merciful regard. Ibn 'Ashur holds that forgetting here means an everlasting abandonment, which the mention of the Fire as their dwelling confirms. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan explain that attributing the meeting to the day is a figure of speech, meaning the meeting with God and His recompense on that day. Several commentators, including Ibn 'Ashur, note that the particle 'as' indicates that the requital corresponds to the deed. Most treat the verse as a rebuke and as a removal of all hope from the disbelievers.

The commentators explain that this verse tells the disbelievers that the punishment befalling them is due to their having mocked the signs of God, meaning the Qur'an and the proofs He established, and to the worldly life which deceived them into thinking there was no afterlife, no resurrection and no reckoning. For this reason they will not be brought out of the Fire, and they will not be asked to win back their Lord's favour, since repentance will be of no use on that Day. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi agree on this general sense, and treat the negation as absolute. On the recitation, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read the verb with an open first letter, while most readers use the passive, and Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan note that the two readings express respectively going out and being taken out. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir explain that to be asked to make amends means that no one will seek to appease them. Ibn al-Qayyim distinguishes this kind of reconciliation, impossible in the hereafter, from the one possible in this world. Many commentators link the verse to the closing praise of God, Lord of the heavens, the earth and the worlds, to whom belongs greatness, the Mighty and the Wise. The scholars do not disagree on the core meaning, only on lexical and recitation details.

This verse closes the surah by declaring that all praise belongs to God alone, because He is the Lord of the heavens, the earth and all worlds. Al-Tabari explains that this praise is owed for the blessings God bestows on His creatures, and that it is directed to Him rather than to idols and the false gods people worship. Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi understand lordship as ownership, sustenance and governance over the heavens, the earth and everything in them, while Ibn Sa'di adds that His lordship over every creature, whom He created and nurtured, is the reason praise is due to Him alone. Al-Baghawi, al-Shawkani and al-Alusi stress that the repetition of the word Lord shows that His lordship over each realm is original and not derived. Ibn Atiyya and al-Qasimi see in the verse a rejection of idolatry and an affirmation of God's divinity. Ibn Ashur links it to the whole surah, presenting it as a conclusion that praises God for the proofs, warnings and favours mentioned earlier. Mujahid, Humayd and Ibn Muhaysin read the word Lord in the nominative, meaning He is Lord, while the majority read it in the genitive as an attribute of God, as al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan report. Al-Razi observes that the phrase all worlds includes every creature, bodies and spirits alike. The commentators agree on the plain meaning: God alone deserves praise because He is the Lord of everything that exists.

This verse closes the passage by proclaiming God's greatness, after announcing that the disbelievers will be left to their punishment for mocking God's signs and for being deceived by the life of this world. Praise belongs to God, Lord of the heavens, the earth and all worlds, and to Him alone belongs greatness (al-kibriya') in the heavens and on earth; He is the Mighty, the Wise. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and the Jalalayn, understand this greatness as majesty, glory and an authority that admits no rival. Al-Mawardi lists several possible meanings of the word: magnificence, sovereignty, nobility or everlasting permanence, and al-Qurtubi also mentions the last of these, adding power and perfection. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari link the praise to the affirmation of God's divinity and to the refutation of idol worship. Ibn 'Ashur sees the particle fa as drawing a conclusion from everything the surah has said about God's blessings and warnings. Several scholars, among them al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and al-Alusi, cite the hadith in which God says that greatness is His garment and majesty His cloak, and that He punishes whoever disputes either with Him. Al-Shinqiti draws from the verse that God alone is to be worshipped in the heavens and on earth. On the divine names, there is broad agreement: al-'Aziz is the Almighty who cannot be overcome, and al-Hakim is the One who places everything in its proper place.
